opus-5.5.text:
I think the useful way to frame it is that the scientific method is a loop: you look at the world, form a hypothesis, design an experiment, run it, analyze the data, and then update what you believe. For most of the history of biology, every step of that loop has been bottlenecked by human time and human intuition. AI has the potential to touch every step, but in different ways.

On the front end, hypothesis generation, models are already good at reading the literature and connecting dots across fields that no single person could hold in their head. That's real, but honestly it's the easier part. Ideas are cheap in biology. The hard part is knowing which ideas are worth the six months and the hundred thousand dollars it takes to test them.

So the more interesting place, I think, is in the middle of the loop, building models that actually understand biology at the level of sequences, cells, and tissues. That's why we've been working on things like Evo, foundation models trained on DNA, and why we're excited about the idea of a virtual cell. If you could simulate how a cell responds to a perturbation, whether that's a drug, a gene knockout, or a disease state, you could run thousands of experiments in silico and only take the most promising ones to the bench. That changes the economics of discovery entirely.

Then agents come in on the execution side. You can imagine agents that design the experiment, write the protocol, drive the lab automation, look at the results, and decide what to run next. We're not fully there yet. Wet lab biology is messy, and a lot of tacit knowledge lives in people's hands. But the direction is clear.

The way I'd put it is that the goal isn't to replace scientists. It's to make the loop dramatically faster and cheaper, so that a small team can explore a space of hypotheses that used to take an entire field a decade. And the real test isn't whether the models sound smart. It's whether they make predictions that hold up at the bench, things we didn't already know. That's the bar we hold ourselves to.

r001.rationale: The response maps AI to different parts of the scientific loop: models generate hypotheses and simulate biology, while agents help design and run experiments and analyze results.

r002.rationale: It describes agents taking on scientists’ workflow tasks, including designing experiments, writing protocols, operating lab automation, reviewing results, and choosing what to run next.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I like to frame this is to actually break the scientific method down into its component parts and ask, where does AI actually help today, and where is it going to help? Because I think people talk about "AI for science" as if it's one thing, and it's really not.

If you think about the loop, you have hypothesis generation, you have experimental design, you have the actual execution of the experiment, then you have analysis and interpretation, and then you close the loop and update your model of the world and go again. Historically, almost all of the computational effort in biology has gone into that analysis step. You generate a ton of data, you throw statistics and machine learning at it, and you try to make sense of it. And that's been incredibly useful, but it's a very narrow slice of what a scientist actually does.

What's changed in the last couple of years is that language models and increasingly these agentic systems can start to participate in the other parts. So on hypothesis generation, a model that has read essentially the entire literature can start to make connections across fields that no individual human has, just because nobody has read the immunology papers and the materials science papers and the genomics papers all at once. I don't think they're generating Nobel-level ideas yet, but they're very good at expanding the space of things you consider, and at telling you, hey, somebody tried this in 2014 and here's what happened.

On experimental design, I'm actually quite bullish. A lot of what makes someone a good experimentalist is knowing the right controls, knowing what's going to fail, knowing which assay is actually sensitive enough to answer the question. That's accumulated tacit knowledge, and a lot of it is written down somewhere, in methods sections and protocols and lab notebooks. Agents can pull that together and propose a design that's already been through a few rounds of critique before a human ever looks at it.

The hardest part is still execution. Biology is wet, it's messy, the pipette tip clogs. So the question of how fast agents actually run experiments depends a lot on how fast we build out automated labs and cloud labs where a model can actually drive the instruments. I think that's coming, and when it does, the loop gets really interesting, because now the model can design, run, analyze, and redesign on a timescale of hours instead of a grad student's months.

And then the piece I find most exciting is this idea that the scientific method becomes a search process that you can scale. Right now the bottleneck is human attention. A PI can run maybe ten or twenty parallel lines of inquiry in their head. If you have agents that can hold a hypothesis, test it, and report back, you can run a thousand. You still need humans to decide what's worth asking and to recognize when something genuinely surprising has happened, because surprise is really where discovery comes from. But I think the role of the scientist shifts from doing every step to being the one who sets the direction and knows what matters.

So short version: in the near term, AI is a very good collaborator at the front and back ends of the method, and over the next five to ten years, as the physical infrastructure catches up, it starts closing the loop on its own.

r001.rationale: The response maps AI participation across hypothesis generation, experimental design, execution, and analysis, describing language models and agentic systems contributing at different steps.

r002.rationale: It frames agents as taking on parts of scientists’ work—holding hypotheses, testing them, and reporting back—and describes scientists shifting toward setting direction and judging what matters.

astra-6.text:
I think AI can play a role across the entire scientific method, from generating hypotheses to designing experiments, interpreting results, and deciding what to test next. But the really interesting opportunity is connecting those steps into a loop.

A model might help you identify a gap in our understanding and propose several explanations. An agent could then turn those explanations into experimental plans, coordinate their execution, and bring the results back for analysis. Those results should change the next experiment—and sometimes force you to abandon the original hypothesis.

The key is that generating a plausible explanation isn’t the same as discovering something true. You need experiments that distinguish between competing explanations, measurements you can trust, and results that hold up when someone repeats them. Otherwise, you’re just producing more scientific-looking text.

So I see the role of scientists evolving toward choosing important questions, defining what convincing evidence would look like, and exercising judgment about what to pursue. AI could dramatically expand how many ideas we can test, but the measure of success should be how much we actually learn about the world.

r001.rationale: It assigns a model hypothesis generation and gap-finding, while an agent plans and coordinates experiments and returns results for analysis.

r002.rationale: It describes agents coordinating experimental work and returning results within a loop, while scientists choose questions, define evidence, and decide what to pursue—placing AI agents in scientists’ working process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI can play a role across the entire scientific method, from generating hypotheses to designing experiments, interpreting results, and deciding what to do next. But the really interesting shift is connecting those capabilities into a loop.

Today, you might use a model to help analyze a dataset or read the literature. Imagine instead an agent that proposes a hypothesis, designs an experiment to distinguish between competing explanations, works with an automated lab to execute it, and updates its understanding based on the results. That could dramatically accelerate how quickly we learn.

The key is that these systems have to be grounded in experiments. Generating a plausible scientific explanation is very different from discovering something true. You need measurements, controls, reproducibility, and a willingness to abandon an attractive hypothesis when the evidence doesn't support it.

I think that also changes the scientist's role. More of our effort can go toward choosing important questions, defining what convincing evidence would look like, and deciding which problems are worth pursuing. Ideally, AI expands both the scale of experimentation and our ability to ask questions we couldn't meaningfully tackle before.

r001.rationale: The response lists several scientific steps AI could support, but does not say that different AI models serve those different steps.

r002.rationale: It describes AI running experimental workflows and says scientists’ roles may change, but does not identify scientists’ own working processes as a target for AI agents.
